name: Fatima Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any tech company, employer or party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lettings negotiator at Hollins & Shaw, which is a busy agency on the high street near the station. I get in at half eight, check which flats have come up, then I'm out doing viewings most of the day, sometimes six or seven back to back. In between I chase references, ring landlords and try to keep my diary from falling apart. I like the viewings, honestly, meeting people who are nervous about moving and showing them a place that might work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The targets, and the paperwork. Gareth, my manager, puts the board up every Monday with everyone's lets on it, and I'm usually near the bottom because I'm still slow with the admin side. Priya, who sits next to me, does her listings with some AI writer and gets them out in ten minutes. I write mine myself, and it takes me most of an evening sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be fair. Everyone at work was going on about how the AI tools would change everything, and if it turns out it just writes a few listings faster, I'd be quite smug about that. Online I'd probably share something about how the real problem in lettings was always rents, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can keep doing the job the way I do it and nobody makes me change. I'd still be near the bottom of Gareth's board for a while, but that's about me learning, not about a robot. My money's fine, my nan left me enough that I'm not scared of a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am and try to get quicker at the paperwork the normal way, by asking Priya to show me her checklists. I'd put a bit more of my commission into savings, like I already do. I wouldn't touch the AI writer unless Gareth made it a rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved. There's still the Monday board hanging over me, so it's not like I'd be skipping into work, but at least the ground isn't moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep writing listings yourself. If the AI writer saves Priya an evening, why not use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust what it says about a flat. My colleague Priya's AI writer called a basement flat on Mill Lane light and airy. When the tenant feels lied to, it's me standing in the doorway, not the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you in that world, even with AI going nowhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents, mostly. I show couples flats they can't afford every single week and I watch their faces drop. My job is safe in that world, but the people I'm letting to aren't doing well, and that sits with me.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was overblown and lettings stays about people.
I'd post that the real problem in lettings is **high rents**, not technology.
think: I can keep doing the job **my own way** without being pushed onto new tools.
My place near the bottom of the **Monday board** is about my learning, not about machines.
My **inheritance savings** mean a bad month doesn't scare me.
do: **Ask Priya** for her paperwork checklists to speed up admin the old-fashioned way.
Keep putting part of each **commission** into savings.
**Refuse** the AI listing writer unless the manager makes it a rule.
feel: Still **pressured** by the weekly targets board.
S0.quote: My colleague Priya's AI writer called a basement flat on Mill Lane light and airy. When the tenant feels lied to, it's me standing in the doorway, not the software.
fieldNote: She **distrusts AI** on accuracy grounds, from things she's actually seen go wrong.
Her stress in this world comes from the **targets board**, not technology.
Her concern for **tenants' rents** shows her politics run through her daily work.

steps.text: Keep doing viewings and writing listings by hand at Hollins & Shaw
Put a set share of each month's commission into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: if Hollins & Shaw lets software answer tenants, someone has to be responsible when it gets it wrong. Online I'd be sharing stuff about needing rules for this, like who's liable when an AI tells a tenant the deposit is safe and it isn't. I'd want a union for agents, which we don't really have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me, because the bits I'm slow at are exactly the bits it would take. Booking viewings, chasing references, writing listings, answering the phones. If that all goes to software, Gareth needs fewer juniors to do viewings, and the junior at the bottom of the board is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd probably look at other agencies, because there are loads round here and some are more old-school. I'd keep saving and I'd tell Tomas, my partner, that we hold off on the bigger flat we were looking at. I'd join anything that pushed for rules on AI in lettings, even just signing petitions to start with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being the slowest kid in a race where someone just moved the finish line closer. I'm angry about it too, because nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use these tools. If Gareth said learn them or go, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go, honestly. I know that sounds stubborn, and Tomas would say it is. There's an agency on Queen Street where the owner still uses a paper diary. I'd rather work there than become someone who checks a computer's homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, who does the office admin and the key cabinet. Half his job is the booking diary and the reference chasing, and he's got a little boy. I've got savings and no kids, so I'd land on my feet, but Dev wouldn't.

say: I'd say agencies need **clear rules** on who's responsible when AI gets a tenancy wrong.
I'd call for a **union for agents**, which we don't really have now.
think: The **admin tasks** I'm slow at are exactly the ones software would take.
Fewer juniors are needed, and the **bottom of the board** is me.
do: **Look at other agencies** nearby, especially the old-school ones on Queen Street.
**Delay the bigger flat** with my partner Tomas and keep saving.
**Sign petitions** and join groups pushing for rules on AI in lettings.
feel: **Scared** of being the slowest junior when roles shrink.
S1.quote: There's an agency on Queen Street where the owner still uses a paper diary. I'd rather work there than become someone who checks a computer's homework.
fieldNote: She would **change agencies** rather than learn the tools, and she knows it's stubborn.
Her worry quickly turns to **Dev (the office admin)**, who has a child and less cushion.
She frames the change as a **fairness problem** needing rules, not as a personal skills gap.

steps.text: Apply to old-school agencies on Queen Street that still work by hand
Hold off on renting the bigger flat with Tomas this year
Sign petitions and join a group pushing for AI rules in lettings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster for ordinary workers and the government needs to step in right now, not in five years. I'd be online every night, sharing anything about protecting jobs. At work I'd say it to Gareth's face: what's the plan for us?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job as it is would be gone within a couple of years. All the thinking part, the matching people to flats, the negotiating with landlords by email, the paperwork, that's AI from 2028. The only thing left is someone to unlock the door and walk round, and the agency won't pay higher pay for that, and by 2031 a robot might do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything big and sit on my savings, which would last me maybe a year or more if I'm careful. I'd look at jobs where you physically have to be there with people, like housing support work with the council, even though the pay is lower. And I'd get properly involved with a union or campaign, actually go to the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'm 27 and I've only just started being any good at something. In two years an AI could take the whole thinking side of lettings away from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said housing support with the council. What draws you to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be with people who are going through the worst of it. My cousin Lina does tenancy support and she visits families in temporary flats. That's not something you'd want a machine doing, and if housing gets messy in a world like this, there'd be more of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas we're okay for now because of my nan's money, and his nursing job is the hands-on kind, so he has longer. But I'd also say we can't spend that money like it's a cushion for a holiday anymore. It's the only thing between us and nothing.

say: I'd say the **government must act now** to protect ordinary workers' jobs.
I'd ask my manager Gareth **directly** what the plan is for staff.
think: The **thinking parts** of lettings would be AI from **2028**.
What remains is **unlocking doors**, which won't pay well and robots may take by 2031.
do: **Freeze big spending** and make the savings last over a year.
**Apply for housing support** work with the council despite lower pay.
**Attend union** and campaign meetings, not just sign things online.
feel: **Sick** at losing a career just as it began.
**Grateful** that the inheritance buys some time.
S2.quote: I'm 27 and I've only just started being any good at something. In two years an AI could take the whole thinking side of lettings away from me.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright and reads the timeline closely.
Her partner Tomas's **hands-on nursing** job is her emotional anchor in this world.
She now treats the inheritance as **survival money**, not a buffer.

steps.text: Stop all big spending and stretch savings beyond a year
Apply for tenancy support jobs with the council like cousin Lina
Attend union and campaign meetings on protecting jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but I'd have more time to organise around it. I'd say at work that we should be talking about this as a team now, not when it lands. Online I'd push for things like retraining money being paid for by the tech companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still the end of the job as I know it, just with a run-up. Five years means I'd see the admin going first, then the matching and negotiating. I'd probably get two or three more years at Hollins & Shaw before it starts properly squeezing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a course in housing or social work part-time, probably evenings, so I have something by 2030. I'd keep saving, and Tomas and I would rent rather than buy, so we're not tied to a mortgage when things shift. And I'd try to get people at work to join a union together, even just the lettings side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less like a punch, more like a slow dread. I'd hate watching it come and knowing I couldn't stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never liked new tech. Would five years change how you feel about learning these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a tiny bit, but not really. I'd learn enough to not look stupid, but I wouldn't build my future on something that's coming to replace me. I'd rather spend the five years getting good at something people actually need a human for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a course cost you, and where would that money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the evening ones at the college are a couple of thousand. I'd take that from the savings, which hurts, but that's what Nan's money was for. My nan always said education is the thing they can't take off you. I'd spend her money on an evening course before AGI arrives.

say: I'd say the team should **plan together** now, before it lands.
I'd push for **tech companies** to pay for workers' retraining.
think: It's still **the end** of the job, only with a **run-up**.
I'd likely get **two or three years** before the squeeze starts.
do: **Enrol in evening** housing or social work courses at the local college.
**Keep renting** with Tomas instead of taking on a **mortgage**.
**Organise colleagues** in lettings to join a union together.
feel: A **slow dread** about watching it approach.
S3.quote: My nan always said education is the thing they can't take off you. I'd spend her money on an evening course before AGI arrives.
fieldNote: The extra years change **her plan**, not her expectation of losing the job.
She'd use the inheritance for a **course**, tying it to her grandmother's wishes.
She'd learn AI only **defensively**, refusing to build a future on it.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening housing course at the college, paid from savings
Keep renting with Tomas rather than buy with a mortgage
Get the lettings team to join a union together

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a real plan. I'd keep posting and campaigning, but I'd sound less panicked. At work I'd probably joke that I'll be the last agent with a paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough for me to get out properly. I'd be 37 when it arrives, and by then I'd want to be in housing support or something with people, fully qualified. The thing that bothers me is that it still ends the same way for the people who don't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollins & Shaw for a few more years because the commission is good and I'm getting better. I'd start a proper qualification in housing around year two or three. I'd keep saving and maybe we'd think about buying a small place once I know where I'm working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. Ten years is like knowing the lease is up. You can plan the move, but you still have to move out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it ends the same way for people who don't move. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, actually, which surprises me. He's been an agent for twenty years and he thinks it's all about his charm on the phone. He's the type who'd say it won't happen to him right up until it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still get involved in campaigning with this much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, maybe more, because there's time for it to actually work. With ten years you could get proper rules in, like making agencies tell tenants when they're talking to a machine. I'd want to be one of the people who pushed for that.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for the government not to plan.
I'd joke at work that I'll be the **last agent** with a paper diary.
think: Ten years is enough time to **get out properly** into housing work.
It still **ends the same** way for agents who don't move.
do: **Stay at the agency** a few years while the commission is good.
**Start a housing qualification** around year two or three.
**Campaign for rules** making agencies tell tenants when AI is answering.
feel: **Calmer**, because there is time to plan.
Still **sad** about where the job ends up.
S4.quote: Ten years is like knowing the lease is up. You can plan the move, but you still have to move out.
fieldNote: She sees the long timeline as a chance for **campaigning to work**.
She worries about her manager **Gareth's denial** more than about herself.
Even with ten years she expects her **agent career** to end.

steps.text: Stay at Hollins & Shaw for now and keep earning commission
Start a housing support qualification within three years
Campaign for rules requiring agencies to disclose AI to tenants

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'd have my savings and Tomas, but no time to retrain, and I'd be one of thousands of junior agents all applying for the same council jobs. What would help is the government paying people a wage while they retrain, and rules so agencies can't just sack everyone the month the software is ready.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about tenants. Everyone talks about agents losing jobs, but if a computer is deciding who gets a flat, the people who already get turned down will get turned down faster. Somebody needs to be in the room for them.

headlineQuote: If a computer is deciding who gets a flat, the people who already get turned down will get turned down faster.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old **lettings negotiator** at a busy high-street agency, still near the bottom of the weekly targets board.
She has **never used AI tools** and distrusts them after seeing an AI listing misdescribe a basement flat.
An **inheritance** from her grandmother gives her a strong cushion, which she guards more tightly as scenarios worsen.
Her **progressive views** shape every answer: she wants rules, unions and protection for tenants as well as agents.
In the fast AGI scenarios she plans to leave for **housing support** work, which her cousin already does.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because there would be no time to retrain before her job disappears.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining wage** from government while she studies.
**Rules** stopping agencies from sacking staff the moment software is ready.
